title: Solar hydrogen production through ambient-pressure seawater splitting

paper_content.abstract: Although polymeric carbon nitride holds promise for solar-driven hydrogen production, its scalability is constrained by reliance on costly vacuum conditions and scarce freshwater supplies. Herein, ultrathin carbon nitride nanosheets are covalently linked to electron-donating pyrene units via π-bridges. The resulting donor–π–acceptor frameworks, featuring a biphenyl π-bridge, exhibit reduced exciton binding energy and long-lived charge-separated states. Insitu spectroscopic and electrochemical analyses collectively demonstrate efficient intramolecular electron transfer and a strengthened built-in internal electric field. Theoretical calculations suggest that electron accumulation on heptazine units may enhance the adsorption of Na⁺/Mg2⁺–triethanolamine complexes, accelerating hole consumption in seawater. As a result, the optimal donor–π–acceptor catalyst shows efficient photocatalytic seawater splitting under ambient pressure and natural sunlight, achieving a hydrogen evolution rate of 134 mmol h−1 g−1. Here, we show a molecular design strategy that advances photocatalytic ambient-pressure seawater splitting and promotes the commercialization of green hydrogen production.
paper_content.introduction:
Although particulate photocatalyst–promoted water splitting enables the sustainable conversion of solar energy into hydrogen as a clean fuel1–3, the related processes typically rely on scarce freshwater supplies and are therefore not easily upscalable4–6. Consequently, considerable attention has been drawn to the solar-driven photocatalytic splitting of seawater—which accounts for ~96.5% of Earth’s water resources—using advanced photocatalysts (e.g., TiO2, g-C3N4, and CdZnS)7–9. Given that these systems are typically operated under low-pressure conditions to suppress back reactions and are also not easily upscalable (Fig. 1a)10, photocatalysts enabling solar-driven hydrogen production through seawater splitting at ambient pressure—such as Domen’s 100m2 array of panel reactors for natural solar hydrogen production—are highly sought after11. Polymeric carbon nitride (CN) materials are well-suited for photocatalytic hydrogen evolution (PHE) because of their flexible chemical structures, tunable band gaps, and cost-effective syntheses12–14. The lone-pair electrons of nitrogen and sp2-hybridized orbitals of CN frameworks result in a high electron density, efficiently suppressing Cl− adsorption and the associated side reactions15. Although these properties make CN a promising platform for photocatalytic seawater splitting, CN-based photocatalysts still exhibit suboptimal PHE performances, largely because of the high binding energy of the singlet Frenkel excitons formed upon excitation. In turn, this high binding energy is due to the strong coulombic interaction in the photogenerated electron–hole pairs, which restricts their dissociation into free charge carriers16. Furthermore, the disordered π-conjugated structure of CN leads to the random migration and rapid recombination of charge carriers17. Rational design strategies reducing the exciton binding energy, enhancing electron delocalization, and improving charge separation in CN are therefore critical for realizing seawater splitting–based PHE under ambient pressure.

The construction of donor–acceptor (D–A)-structured organic semiconductors—such as covalent organic frameworks18, conjugated polymers19, and conjugated molecules20—is an effective strategy for reducing the exciton binding energy and promoting exciton dissociation. This effect arises from intramolecular charge transfer (ICT) due to the electron push-pull effect of the D and A units21. Consequently, various D (e.g., thiophene, triazine, and methoxyphenyl) and A (e.g., benzene, anthraquinone, and benzothiadiazole) groups have been incorporated into CN to construct D–A-structured frameworks. Such modifications facilitate exciton dissociation and enhance charge separation between CN and D or A units upon excitation, thereby improving photocatalytic activity (Fig. 1b)22,23. The electronegativity of CN promotes the adsorption of protons, because of the positive-negative electrostatic attraction7. This concurrent accumulation of electrons and protons favors rapid proton reduction and, hence, hydrogen production. Therefore, by incorporating electron-donating rather than electron-accepting groups into CN frameworks, one can not only preserve the hydrogen production sites but also promote the continuous transfer of excited electrons to the CN backbone and thus optimize the intermediate adsorption/desorption energy and reduce the energy barrier of the PHE reaction24. However, the electron-donating groups examined to date, such as thiophene, triazine, and methoxyphenyl moieties, exhibit weak electron delocalization ability because of their narrow aromatic hydrocarbon structures25, and are therefore inefficient in modulating electron delocalization within CN.

Pyrene, a well-known strongly electron-delocalized chromophore due to its four fused benzene rings of an alternating polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon25, featuring a wide π-conjugated structure that ensures rapid electron transfer and efficient light harvesting, has been extensively explored in the construction of D–A-type covalent organic frameworks for photocatalytic hydrogen peroxide and hydrogen production26–29. However, the direct linking of CN with pyrene units results in low photocatalytic activities29–31, probably because the limited electron delocalization within the CN–pyrene structure restricts photoexcited charge migration between the two components. In the case of D–A-type covalent organic frameworks, the introduction of π-bridges between the D and A units effectively extends π-conjugation and thereby enhances electron delocalization and facilitates ICT32–34. Furthermore, larger delocalization systems and longer distances between the D and A units hinder the recombination of photogenerated charge carriers35. Hence, π-bridge-induced electron delocalization between CN and pyrene units can be leveraged to design D–π–A-structured CN frameworks with reduced exciton binding energies, extended π-conjugated systems, improved charge transport properties, and, hence, high PHE performances under ambient pressure.

In this work, we introduce D–π–A-structured CN frameworks by covalently incorporating electron-donating pyrene units into ultrathin CN nanosheet (UCN) using π-bridges (a single benzene ring, biphenyl moiety, or a benzene ring linked to an acetylene group; Fig. 1c, d). Through a combination of temperature-dependent photoluminescence (TD-PL), femtosecond transient absorption spectroscopy (fs-TAS), insitu X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS), and theoretical calculations, we quantitatively demonstrate that the biphenyl π-bridged UPy2 framework achieves a significantly reduced exciton binding energy, a prolonged charge-carrier lifetime, and a strengthened intramolecular electric field. Moreover, density functional theory (DFT) reveals that the enhanced electron accumulation on heptazine units promotes the adsorption of seawater cations and their complexes with triethanolamine, thereby accelerating hole-consumption. As a result, UPy2, featuring a biphenyl moiety as π-bridges, exhibits the highest PHE performance in natural seawater under simulated solar light (AM 1.5G) and ambient pressure, achieving a hydrogen production rate of 82 mmol h−1 g−1. A scalable 20 cm diameter disk reactor with this photocatalyst demonstrated a PHE rate of 134 mmol g−1 h−1 in natural seawater under natural sunlight, further demonstrating the scalability of this photocatalytic system and highlighting its potential for practical seawater hydrogen production.
paper_content.results:
Design, synthesis, and characterization of the UPy frameworks
Three D–π–A-structured CN frameworks (Fig. 1d)—UPy1, UPy2, and UPy3—were obtained by covalently linking CN with π-pyrene-π molecules (Py1, Py2, and Py3) (Supplementary Fig. 1), each featuring a pyrene core (D unit), π-bridge (a single benzene ring, biphenyl moiety, or a benzene ring linked to an acetylene group), and four aldehyde groups as Schiff-base reactive sites. The electrostatic surface potential (ESP) distributions of these molecules (Supplementary Fig. 1 and Supplementary Data 1) suggested that negative potentials were primarily located around the pyrene units, favoring electron donation during excitation36. Among them, Py2 exhibited the largest molecular dipole moment (3.52 D), thus achieving the strongest electric-field polarization and potentially facilitating charge transfer37–39. The covalent linking of the heptazine rings and π-pyrene-π molecules yielded frameworks (UPy1, UPy2, and UPy3) with asymmetric ESP distributions indicative of the formation of localized electric fields that may promote electron delocalization and charge separation (Fig. 1d and Supplementary Data 2). This functionalization resulted in the potential at the center of the heptazine ring becoming more negative, suggesting an electron transfer from the pyrene unit to CN. The spatial distributions of the corresponding energy levels (Supplementary Figs. 2 and 3 and Supplementary Data 3 and 4) indicated that in CN and Py1–Py3, the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) and lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO) were largely localized on the heptazine ring and pyrene units, respectively, which could hinder charge separation under excitation. In contrast, the UPy frameworks exhibited a clear HOMO–LUMO separation. This separation was most pronounced for UPy2, in which case the LUMO was distributed over the heptazine ring and π-bridge, and the HOMO was primarily located on the pyrene unit. This spatial orbital separation could facilitate electron transfer from the pyrene unit to the heptazine ring via the π-bridge upon excitation40–42.

The covalent integration of UCN with the π-pyrene-π molecules is illustrated in Fig. 2a. UCN was synthesized by the thermal oxidation of bulk CN obtained via the thermal polymerization of urea. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) imaging revealed that bulk CN exhibited a thick layered structure (Supplementary Fig. 4), whereas UCN displayed a thin porous structure (Fig. 2b, c). Upon ultrasonication, UCN fragmented into small, irregular pieces, as displayed in the SEM image (Supplementary Fig. 5). These fragments were subsequently covalently linked into large blocky-like structures by Py2 molecules via a Schiff-base reaction, forming UPy2 framework (Fig. 2d, e). The rod-like Py1 and Py2 particles and lamellar Py3 particles, each several micrometers in size (Supplementary Fig. 6), were not observed in the UPy frameworks (Fig. 2b, c; Supplementary Fig. 7), which suggests the formation of uniform covalent links between the π-pyrene-π molecules and UCN.

The X-ray diffraction (XRD) patterns of UCN and the UPy frameworks (Supplementary Fig. 9) exhibited two characteristic peaks at approximately 13.0° and 27.4° corresponding to the (100) in-plane repeating units and (002) interlayer stacking of the conjugated motifs of CN, respectively43. The absence of π-pyrene-π molecule signals in the UPy framework patterns was ascribed to the uniform covalent bonding of these molecules with UCN. The Fourier transform infrared (FTIR) spectra of UCN, UPy1, UPy2, and UPy3 (Supplementary Fig. 10a) exhibited peaks corresponding to –NH groups (3000–3500 cm−1), aromatic C–N heterocycles (1300–1700 cm−1), and triazine rings in CN (810 cm−1)44. The –NH band intensities of UPy1, UPy2, and UPy3 were lower than that of UCN, indicating the consumption of –NH groups during covalent bonding with the π-pyrene-π molecules. No characteristic stretching vibrations of aromatic groups (–C=C–/–C–C–) in the π-pyrene-π molecules (typically 800–1700 cm−1) were observed in the UPy spectra, probably because of their overlap with imine (–C=N–) stretching bands. A weak –C≡C– peak at 2200 cm−1 was observed for UPy3 (Supplementary Fig. 10c). Additionally, the increased intensities and shifts of the peaks at 1407 and 1460 cm−1 observed for UPy1, UPy2, and UPy3 confirmed the formation of covalent links between UCN and the π-pyrene-π molecules45 (Supplementary Fig. 10b). In addition, the Raman spectra (Supplementary Fig. 11) revealed that UCN and UPy frameworks exhibited characteristic vibration modes of CN heterocycles at 470, 708, 770, 1213, 1232, 1310, and 1350 cm−1. The additional bands at ~1400 and 1560 cm−1 corresponded to C–C/C=C vibrations of the pyrene units in the UPy frameworks. Furthermore, the additional peaks near 1610 cm−1 in UPy frameworks were assigned to C=N bond vibrations, providing additional evidence for the successful covalent linkage of Py1, Py2, and Py3 to UCN46. The 13C nuclear magnetic resonance spectra of UCN, UPy1, UPy2, and UPy3 showed two prominent peaks at 165.4 and 156.5 ppm, assigned to the C(1) atoms of N=C–(N)2 and C(2) atoms of N=C–N(NHx) in heptazine units, respectively47 (Supplementary Fig. 12). The UPy spectra displayed additional peaks in the range of 120–140 ppm, attributed to sp2-bonded skeletal carbons, and weak peaks near 150 ppm, ascribed to covalent linkages between UCN and the π-pyrene-π molecules48.

The deconvoluted C 1s X-ray photoelectron spectrum of UCN (Supplementary Fig. 13a) featured peaks at 284.80 and 288.06 eV, which were assigned to sp2-C bonds originating from extrinsic carbon impurities (used as a calibration reference) and sp2-C bonds in the heptazine rings (N–C=N), respectively. The increased intensity of the former peak observed for UPy1, UPy2, and UPy3 indicated the incorporation of aromatic units from the π-pyrene-π molecules49, consistent with the higher C/N molar ratio observed for these frameworks by elemental analysis (Supplementary Table 1). Elemental analysis was further employed to estimate the π-pyrene-π contents in the UPy frameworks, yielding values of approximately 1.84 wt% for UPy1, 2.87 wt% for UPy2, and 2.26 wt% for UPy3. These values are lower than the nominal feeding ratio (0.1 g UCN vs. 5 mg π-pyrene-π molecules), likely because a fraction of the π-pyrene-π molecules did not successfully couple to the UCN. The new UPy peak at 286.60–286.50 eV was ascribed to C=N bonds and confirmed the formation of covalent linkages50. The deconvoluted N 1s spectra of UCN and the UPy frameworks featured four peaks corresponding to π* excitations, terminal N–H groups, tertiary nitrogen in N–(C)3 moieties, and sp2-hybridized nitrogen in C=N–C moieties44 (Supplementary Fig. 13b). The decrease in the fractional area of the N–H peak observed for the UPy frameworks was ascribed to the consumption of N–H groups during covalent bond formation with the π-pyrene-π molecules51.

The C K-edge near-edge X-ray absorption fine structure (NEXAFS) spectra of UCN and UPy2 (Fig. 2f) displayed peaks at 288.5 and 288.7 eV, respectively, attributed to the π* (N–C=N) sp2-hybridized states of CN. The peak at ~285.6 eV observed for UPy2 was assigned to π*(C–C/C=C) transitions from the aromatic units of the Py2 moiety. The stronger peak at ~286.2 eV, attributed to π*(C–N=C), suggested the presence of imine linkages between UCN and Py252. The N K-edge NEXAFS spectra of UCN and UPy2 (Fig. 2g) featured peaks near 400.0, 402.0, and 403.0 eV, corresponding to nitrogen in C=N–C, N–(C)3, and C–NHx moieties, respectively53. The spectrum of UPy2 also showed a weak peak at 406.3 eV, which was assigned to the C–N σ* orbital and confirmed the presence of C=N bonds54. Together, these results corroborate the formation of covalent linkages in the UPy frameworks.

PHE performances
PHE tests were conducted in a glass-closed gas system under a negative pressure and visible-light illumination (λ>400 nm, 100 mW cm−2) at 281 K (Supplementary Figs. 14 and 15). Deionized (DI) water containing 10 vol% TEOA was used as a sacrificial reagent, and 3 wt% Pt was loaded onto the catalyst via photoinduced deposition as a hydrogen evolution cocatalyst (see “Methods” for details). As shown in Supplementary Fig. 16, the PHE rates of UPy1, UPy2, and UPy3 were markedly higher than those of pure CN, UCN, or the individual π-pyrene-π molecules. For each UPy framework, the catalysts prepared with the optimal π-pyrene-π molecules (UPy1-5, UPy2-5, and UPy3-3) achieved the highest PHE rates. Further increases in π-pyrene-π contents led to decreased PHE rates, likely due to aggregation of excess π-pyrene-π molecules, which partially shield surface active sites. Among all the UPy frameworks, the UPy2-5 exhibited the highest PHE rate of 17.85 mmol h−1 g−1—357, 64, and 40 times higher than those of Py2 (0.05 mmol h−1 g−1), CN (0.28 mmol h−1 g−1), and UCN (0.44 mmol h−1 g−1), respectively. Although UPy1 and UPy3 also exhibited enhanced PHE performances after Py1 and Py3 loading optimization, their PHE rates remained lower than that of UPy2, possibly because of the stronger electron transfer from pyrene to CN facilitated by the longer π-conjugated chain in UPy2.

Compared with the covalent linkage–containing UPy2, UPy2-π-π, which featured interfacial π-π interactions only, exhibited a lower PHE rate of 4.12 mmol h−1 g−1. This result highlights the critical role of well-regulated charge transfer at the covalent interface of the D-π-A-type UPy2 in achieving efficient PHE. Similarly, a control sample in which Py2 was covalently linked to the edges of bulk CN (CPy2) showed a low PHE rate of 4.94 mmol h−1 g−1, which confirmed the advantage of reassembling UCN via covalent bonding with Py2. During long-term stability testing, the PHE rate of UPy2 (Supplementary Fig. 17) decreased from 17.85 mmol h−1 g−1 in the first cycle to 14.20 mmol h−1 g−1 in the fourth cycle, probably because of the detachment of unstable Py2 molecules from the catalyst surface, and remained stable in the subsequent 11 cycles. This behavior indicates the high long-term stability of UPy2 for PHE applications.

PHE experiments under ambient pressure without inert-gas protection were conducted in a Pyrex vessel connected to a gas circulator using DI water, simulated seawater (3.5 wt% aqueous NaCl), and natural seawater as reaction media under simulated solar light illumination (AM 1.5G, 100 mW cm−2) at 298 K (Supplementary Figs. 18–21). TEOA (10 vol%) and Pt (3 wt%) were used as the sacrificial reagent and cocatalyst, respectively. All UPy frameworks, as well as UPy2-π-π and CPy2, exhibited notable PHE performances under ambient pressure (Fig. 3a and Supplementary Fig. 22). In contrast, neither CN nor UCN produced detectable amounts of hydrogen in any of the media, probably because the small amount of the generated hydrogen could not overcome surface tension to escape from the liquid phase. The π-pyrene-π molecules also exhibited negligible PHE activity, as evidenced by the absence of detectable H₂ signals in the gas chromatography (GC) spectra (Supplementary Fig. 23). UPy2 exhibited the highest activity among the tested catalysts, achieving a PHE rate of 44.50 mmol h−1 g−1 in seawater. The lower PHE rates observed in DI water and NaCl solution suggested the advantageous effect of metal cations present in seawater on PHE.

To further optimize the PHE performance of UPy2 in seawater, we varied the temperature, catalyst mass, Pt loading, TEOA concentration, and sacrificial reagent type. The PHE activity increased with the increasing temperature because of the concomitant acceleration of charge and mass transfer (Supplementary Fig. 24). The non-normalized PHE rate increased with the increasing catalyst mass up to 20 mg and then plateaued (Supplementary Fig. 25a). The catalyst mass–normalized PHE rate reached a maximum at 20 mg and then declined (Supplementary Fig. 25b). These results indicate that the absolute and catalyst mass–normalized hydrogen production rates were not strictly proportional to catalyst mass, probably because of limitations in light absorption and reactant/product mass transport55 (Supplementary Fig. 25c). Thus, the optimal catalyst mass was identified as 20 mg. Under this condition, the PHE rate increased with the increasing Pt content (Supplementary Fig. 26a), equaling 71.65 and 79.13 mmol h−1 g−1 at 5 and 10 wt% Pt, respectively. In addition, UPy2 without Pt loading exhibited negligible PHE activity, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 26b. Considering cost-effectiveness, the optimal Pt loading was selected as 5 wt%. Under these conditions, the PHE rate increased and then decreased with the increasing TEOA content, peaking at 5 vol% TEOA (82.00 mmol h−1 g−1) (Supplementary Fig. 27a). UPy2 achieved a competitive PHE performance compared with previously reported systems under similar conditions (Supplementary Table 2). Even at a low TEOA content of 1 vol%, the PHE rate remained high at 50.19 mmol h−1 g−1, which underscores the essential role of TEOA in PHE for seawater splitting. Unlike most ambient-pressure photocatalytic systems that require inert-gas protection6,56, the UPy2 system maintains high PHE activity under an air atmosphere, without N₂ or Ar purging, highlighting its strong potential for practical applications. In contrast, no hydrogen production was observed for pure seawater (Supplementary Fig. 27b, c) or in the presence of alternative sacrificial reagents, including 10 vol% methanol, 50 mM ascorbic acid, and 0.25 M Na2S/0.35 M Na2SO3 (Supplementary Fig. 27b). These results emphasize the effectiveness of TEOA, which may be due to its coordination with metal cations in seawater enabling efficient hole consumption.

The effect of irradiation wavelength on the PHE performance of UPy2 in seawater under ambient pressure was investigated using catalyst, Pt, and TEOA loadings of 20 mg, 5 wt%, and 5 vol%, respectively. The apparent quantum efficiency (AQE) followed the light absorption profile of UPy2 (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Table 3) and reached 4.77% at 450 nm in seawater. The lower values obtained in the NaCl solution (1.46%) and DI water (0.24%) highlight the high potential of UPy2 for efficient solar-driven seawater splitting under ambient pressure. During long-term stability tests at ambient pressure and 298 K, the PHE rate of UPy2 peaked during the third hour and gradually declined thereafter (Fig. 3c). Following evacuation at the ninth and seventeenth hours, the rate recovered and increased to ~30 mmol h−1 g−1. The reduced activity in the final two cycles compared with that in the first cycle was ascribed to the precipitation of Mg2+ from seawater as Mg(OH)2 on the UPy2 surface, which impeded catalytic activity.

The chemical composition and morphology of UPy2 after PHE in DI water and seawater were analyzed by XRD, FTIR, high-resolution XPS, SEM, and TEM. The XRD patterns and FTIR, C 1s, and N 1s spectra of the two samples were identical to those of pristine UPy2, revealing that the crystalline and molecular structures remained unchanged (Supplementary Figs. 28 and 29). Distinct Mg(OH)2 peaks and weak Ca(OH)2 peaks were observed in the XRD pattern of the seawater-processed sample, indicating the co-precipitation of Mg2+ and Ca2+ during the PHE reaction (Supplementary Fig. 28a). SEM and TEM imaging revealed that the morphology of UPy2 was preserved in both cases (Supplementary Figs. 30 and 31). Additional nanosheets were observed on the surface of the seawater-processed sample, confirming the formation of Mg(OH)2 and Ca(OH)2. The reduction of H+ to H2 during PHE increased the local alkalinity at the catalyst surface, promoting Mg(OH)2 and Ca(OH)2 precipitation. The predominance of Mg(OH)2, accompanied with trace amounts of Ca(OH)2, was further confirmed by Mg 1s, Ca 2p, and O 1s XPS spectra (Supplementary Fig. 32). The absorption spectra of UPy2 after PHE in DI water and seawater remained largely unchanged except for the enhanced absorption at 550–800 nm, which was attributed to photo-deposited Pt nanoparticles on the catalyst surface (Supplementary Fig. 33).

The presence of Pt on the catalyst surface was confirmed by XRD and high-resolution Pt 4f spectra. The XRD patterns (Supplementary Fig. 28a) featured a weak peak at 46° due to the (200) plane of cubic Pt nanoparticles. The Pt 4f spectra of the water- and seawater-processed samples featured three sets of doublets at 73.3/73.2, 70.3/70.2, and 76.2/75.5 eV, indicating the partial reduction of Pt4+ to Pt⁰ and Pt2+, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 29c). TEM imaging revealed the uniform distribution of Pt nanoparticles on the UPy2 surface (Supplementary Fig. 34). Particle size analysis revealed that the PHE reaction in seawater promoted the formation of smaller Pt particles (mean size = 6.7 nm, cf. 13.9 nm in DI water). These smaller Pt nanoparticles probably contributed to the enhanced performance by increasing the interfacial area and facilitating charge transfer between Pt and UPy2. This effect could have resulted from the uniform adsorption of metal cation–TEOA complexes on the catalyst surface, which rapidly captured photogenerated holes, accelerated charge separation, and promoted localized electron accumulation, driving the reduction of Pt4+ to smaller Pt nanoparticles.

When the suspension obtained after the PHE reaction in seawater was transferred to a beaker and illuminated with an Xe lamp, numerous bubbles formed within 2 min and adhered to the inner wall of the beaker (Fig. 3d and Supplementary Movie 1). Furthermore, the exposure of the beaker to natural sunlight also produced abundant bubbles (Fig. 3e and Supplementary Movie 2). A blank control experiment was also conducted by exposing the same reaction solution to outdoor sunlight in the absence of a catalyst, during which no bubble formation was observed (Supplementary Movie 3). A disk-shaped reactor (20 cm diameter, 10 cm height) was designed to accurately evaluate PHE activity using natural seawater under ambient pressure (Fig. 3f and Supplementary Fig. 35). In this setup, UPy2 produced ~170 mL of hydrogen within 1 h (10:00 a.m. to 11:00 a.m.; Supplementary Movie 4), achieving a PHE rate of 134 mmol h−1 g−1. To verify the gas composition, the gas collected from the reactor equipped with a gas collection bag (Supplementary Fig. 36) was analyzed using GC spectrum. A distinct hydrogen peak was observed in Supplementary Fig. 37, confirming that hydrogen evolution occurred under outdoor sunlight irradiation. Furthermore, the successful ignition of gas collected from the disk-shaped reactor (20 cm diameter, 3 cm height) connected to a gas-collecting bag, as shown in Supplementary Movie 5 and Fig. 38, confirms hydrogen generation from PHE in seawater under natural sunlight and ambient pressure57. These results confirm the potential of UPy2 for photocatalytic hydrogen generation from seawater under ambient pressure.

Optical properties and band structures
To further rationalize the high PHE performance of UPy2, we examined the light absorption properties and band structures of UCN, the π-pyrene-π molecules, and the UPy frameworks using ultraviolet–visible diffuse reflectance spectroscopy, ultraviolet photoelectron spectroscopy (UPS), and valence band XPS (VB-XPS). Owing to the broadband absorption of visible light by the π-pyrene-π molecules, their covalent linkage to UCN substantially enhanced its visible-light absorption capacity (Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 39). The spectrum of UPy2 exhibited a pronounced absorption increase in the 420–550 nm range compared with that of UCN. Additionally, the optical absorption edges of the UPy frameworks were red-shifted relative to those of UCN, which was attributed to the expansion of the π-conjugated structure due to the covalent integration of the π-pyrene-π molecules.

The band gaps (Eg) of UCN, UPy1, UPy2, and UPy3 were determined using the transformed Kubelka–Munk function as 2.97, 2.93, 2.81, and 2.89 eV, respectively (Fig. 4b and Supplementary Fig. 40). The valence band (VB) maximum (EVB) and conduction band (CB) minimum (ECB) of UCN were determined as +2.09 and −0.88 eV vs. the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE), respectively14, based on the corresponding ultraviolet photoelectron spectrum (Supplementary Fig. 41). Based on the VB-XPS profiles of UPy1, UPy2, and UPy3 (Supplementary Fig. 42), the corresponding VB maxima were shifted to 2.31, 2.34, and 2.17 eV vs. RHE, respectively. The CB positions of UPy1, UPy2, and UPy3 were calculated as −0.62, −0.47, −0.72 eV vs. RHE, respectively, according to ECB = −(Eg − EVB) (Fig. 4b). The VB potentials of the UPy frameworks were more positive than that of UCN, suggesting a stronger driving force for the oxidation of TEOA.

Mechanism of charge separation
The photoluminescence quantum yield (PLQY) was employed as an indirect indicator of photogenerated carrier transport efficiency. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 43, pristine UCN exhibited a PLQY of 3.61%, whereas the lower PLQYs of UPy1 (2.12%) and UPy2 (0.39%) indicated that covalent coupling with Py1 or Py2 promoted charge transfer and suppressed radiative recombination58. In contrast, the higher PLQY of UPy3 (9.11%) arises from emissive charge transfer states near 600 nm that enhance radiative recombination but compete with charge separation. The high exciton binding energies (Eb) of organic photocatalysts substantially hinder the dissociation of excitons into free electrons and holes, limiting photocatalytic performance59. This restricted exciton dissociation is the primary reason for the low activity of polymeric UCN catalysts. Herein, TD-PL measurements were conducted to investigate exciton dissociation behavior and determine Eb. The PL intensity decreased with an increase in temperature from 83 to 298 K, indicating enhanced exciton dissociation (Fig. 4c–f). The corresponding Eb values were calculated as ~60 meV for UCN, ~50 meV for UPy1, ~28 meV for UPy2, and ~32 meV for UPy3 by fitting the PL spectra using the Arrhenius equation (see “Methods” for details). These results highlight the promotional effects of the UPy frameworks on exciton dissociation and their exceptional charge carrier generation abilities60.

Inefficient charge transfer and separation is another key bottleneck limiting PHE activity. To address this problem, we examined the effect of covalently linking UCN with the π-pyrene-π molecules on the photoinduced charge transfer and separation properties. The PL spectrum of UCN recorded under 365 nm excitation (Fig. 4g) exhibited a strong emission peak at ~460 nm corresponding to the radiative decay of the lowest excited state. The weakening of this peak in the spectra of the UPy frameworks indicated the suppression of radiative recombination due to enhanced charge transfer between UCN and the π-pyrene-π molecules, which enhanced non-radiative carrier recombination. Moreover, shortened lifetimes (i.e., accelerated PL decay) were observed for the UPy frameworks under 365 nm excitation: 7.22 ns for UCN, 5.46 ns for UPy1, 3.50 ns for UPy2, and 4.39 ns for UPy3 (Fig. 4h and Supplementary Table 4). These results suggest that photoinduced electron transfer from the electron-donating pyrene units to UCN accelerated charge transfer in the UCN matrix.

UPy2 exhibited the highest photocurrent response, the smallest arc radius and resistance (Supplementary Fig. 44 and Supplementary Table 5), which indicated that the covalent linkage of Py2 with UCN enabled charge transfer more efficiently than that in UCN, UPy1, and UPy323. The surface charge transfer properties were further investigated using surface photovoltage (SPV) measurements. UPy2 displayed strong positive SPV signals characteristic of an n-type semiconductor, including a pronounced peak in the 300–520 nm range (Supplementary Fig. 45). This enhanced SPV response indicates improved charge transfer efficiency and electron accumulation on the surface and can be attributed to electron transfer from Py2 to UCN61. To elucidate the driving force of charge transfer, the magnitudes of the built-in internal electric field (BIEF) were quantified using surface charge density (Supplementary Fig. 44b) and SPV measurements (Supplementary Fig. 45)62. As shown in Fig. 4i, all UPy frameworks exhibited higher BIEF intensities than UCN, with UPy2 displaying the strongest field, which is 8.2 times higher than that of UCN. The highly symmetric structure of UCN resulted in a weak BIEF, limiting efficient electron–hole separation63,64. In contrast, covalent incorporation of π-pyrene-π molecules into UCN induced a D–π–A configuration in the UPy frameworks, significantly enhancing electron delocalization and ICT. This structural design effectively strengthens the BIEF and contributes to the high charge-separation efficiency observed for UPy265. Photo-assisted Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) provided additional insights into surface charge dynamics. UCN showed a surface potential decrease of 15 mV under illumination, which indicated a reduction in photogenerated electron density (Supplementary Fig. 46a–c). In contrast, UPy1, UPy2, and UPy3 exhibited surface potential increases of 4, 67, and 51 mV, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 46d–l), which suggested that the photoinduced electrons in the UPy frameworks mainly migrated to the surface, driven by enhanced electron transfer from the π-pyrene-π molecules to UCN66. Subsequently, we conducted electron paramagnetic resonance spin-trap experiments using 5,5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline n-oxide (DMPO) to detect the reactive oxygen species generated during the photocatalytic process. The signal intensity of the DMPO–•O2− adduct produced under illumination followed the order UPy2>UPy3>UPy1>UCN (Supplementary Fig. 47). The strongest signal was observed for UPy2, confirming its efficient charge separation and surface electron accumulation, indicative of an enhanced electron reduction capability61.

Insights into charge transfer kinetics
The charge transfer dynamics were further probed by fs-TAS, with measurements conducted using 325 nm laser pulses and a white-light probe (350–650 nm). Supplementary Fig. 48 and Fig. 5a, b present the two-dimensional contour plots and kinetic profiles of UCN and UPy2. Positive signals in the 500–750 nm range indicate excited-state absorption (ESA) from trapped photogenerated electrons67. The corresponding kinetic decay traces at 700 nm, a representative ESA wavelength, are shown in Fig. 5c, d. Pristine UCN exhibited three decay components, namely τ1 = 2.5 ps—corresponding to rapid electron capture by intrinsic shallow-trap (ST) states, τ2 = 31.6 ps—associated with slower band-edge exciton recombination, and τ3 = 443.0 ps—ascribed to long-lived charge separation via deep-trap (DT) states (Fig. 5e)68. The inclusion of a long-time offset constant (y0) further highlight the contribution of persistent photogenerated carriers that sustain photocatalytic activity. In contrast, UPy2 exhibited four decay components: τ1 = 4.1 ps, τ2 = 52.5 ps, τ3 = 742.1 ps, τ4 = 1683 ps, indicating that D–A covalent coupling substantially slows recombination and enhances charge separation. Specifically, τ1 is assigned to ultrafast ICT between the UCN and pyrene unit; τ2 corresponds to band-edge recombination; τ3 reflects deep-trap stabilization of separated charges; and τ4 represents a long-lived charge-separated (CS) state extending beyond the ps regime69,70. The emergence of these slower components (τ3 and τ4) confirms the markedly improved electron–hole separation efficiency in UPy271. The charge transfer dynamics of UPy1 and UPy3 were also evaluated using fs-TAS (Supplementary Fig. 49). The covalent linkage of pyrene to the CN framework through alternative π-bridges (a single benzene ring or a benzene-linked alkynyl group) also helped prolong the charge carrier lifetime. The longest average lifetime was observed for UPy2, which suggested that the incorporation of a biphenyl moiety π-bridge most effectively suppressed charge recombination by enhancing electron delocalization between CN and pyrene.

Given the strongly pump fluence-dependent kinetics on CN-based systems, fs-TAS measurements for both UCN and UPy2 were conducted at four pump energy densities: 0.24, 0.37, 0.96, and 1.94 mJ cm−2. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 50 and Fig. 5f, g, both UCN and UPy2 exhibited pronounced pump-fluence-dependent fs-TAS decay kinetics. The initial ΔA amplitudes at ~500 fs increased linearly with excitation fluence, with slopes close to unity (>0.96), indicating fluence-independent initial electron generation (Fig. 5h). All decay traces were well fitted by a power-law model, ΔA(t) = α·(t−t₀)−β, with β consistently falling within 0.20±0.02 (Supplementary Table 6)72. Under linear-response conditions, the transient absorption signal ΔA(t) was proportional to the population of the long-lived charge carriers contributing to the probed band. Accordingly, the parameter α reflects the carrier density at the onset of the power-law regime. Across all fluences, UPy2 displayed substantially larger α values than UCN, demonstrating that UPy2 sustained a higher density of long-lived charge-separated carriers immediately after excitation73. The extracted half-times (t0.5) further revealed distinct recombination dynamics. Both UCN and UPy2 displayed shorter t0.5 at higher fluences, consistent with fluence-enhanced bimolecular or higher-order recombination processes. However, under identical excitation conditions, UPy2 consistently showed longer t0.5 than UCN, indicating slower carrier recombination and more efficient stabilization of long-lived charge carriers74. Additional differences were observed in the residual electron population at ~2 ns. For UPy2, the fraction of long-lived electrons decreased from 31% at low fluence to 21.7% at high fluence, whereas UCN showed negligible variation across the same range. The stronger fluence dependence in UPy2 arises from its larger initial carrier densities, which accelerate bimolecular recombination at high fluence. Importantly, the reduced residual electrons at high fluence do not imply weaker charge separation but rather reflect redistribution of an initial larger carrier population into long- and short-lived recombination channels. In contrast, the weak fluence response of UCN was consistent with its inherently limited charge-separation capability and the absence of an efficient ICT pathway72. Collectively, the larger α values, longer decay half-times, and stronger fluence-dependent modulation of long-lived electrons in UPy2 confirmed its markedly enhanced electron–hole separation compared with UCN.

To further investigate how visible-light excitation influences the excited-state dynamics of the D–π–A UPy systems, the fs-TAS responses of the three π-pyrene-π molecules and the corresponding UPy frameworks under 450 nm excitation were compared (Supplementary Figs. 51 and 52). The π-pyrene-π molecules displayed a strong stimulated-emission (SE) band at ~600 nm and broad ESA extending to ~750 nm. These features were markedly suppressed in UPy frameworks. The reduced SE and ESA intensities indicated the rapid formation of an ICT state between the pyrene units and UCN. Correspondingly, the kinetic traces of the UPy frameworks exhibited significantly slower decay dynamics with prominent long-lived components, consistent with the presence of stabilized ICT or charge-separated state75. These findings demonstrated that covalent linkage of π-pyrene-π molecules to UCN enhances electron–hole separation and prolongs excited-state lifetimes under visible-light excitation.

The synchronous illumination XPS measurements were conducted to investigate the charge transfer dynamics of the UPy frameworks under illumination. Under visible-light irradiation, the N–C=N peak in the C 1s spectrum and all peaks in the N 1s spectrum of UCN noticeably shifted to higher binding energies, which indicated a reduction in the electron density around the heptazine ring (Supplementary Fig. 53). In contrast, only minimal shifts to lower binding energies were observed for the C 1s and N 1s spectra of UPy2, suggesting that photogenerated electrons were transferred from the pyrene units of Py2 to the heptazine ring of UCN, increasing the electron density at the ring76. The substantial negative shift in the π-excitation features of UPy2 indicated an increased π-electron density, attributed to the extended π-conjugated structure of this framework. To further highlight the mechanistic significance of covalent D–A linkage, the charge transfer properties of UPy2 and UPy2-π-π were compared. Evidence from PL quenching, faster PL decay, and significantly prolonged fs-TAS decay lifetime (Supplementary Fig. 54) confirmed that UPy2 suppresses radiative and non-radiative recombination far more effectively than UPy2-π-π. This strengthened electronic coupling and ICT efficiency enabled by covalent bonding are key factors underlying the improved PHE performance77.

The kinetic behavior of excited-state electrons and holes in UCN and UPy2 was investigated using time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) calculations. The UCN model suggested a disordered distribution of excited electrons and holes, whereas the UPy2 model showed a more pronounced tendency toward spatial separation, with excited electrons and holes localized on the heptazine ring and pyrene units, respectively (Supplementary Fig. 55 and Supplementary Data 5). Furthermore, UPy2 model structures containing two or three heptazine ring segments covalently linked to one Py molecule (U2Py2 and U3Py2) were constructed, and their excited-state charge distributions were investigated in Supplementary Figs. 56 and 57, and Supplementary Data 6 and 7. These models exhibited similar trends of spatial separation of excited electrons and holes, localized on the heptazine ring and pyrene units, respectively. This spatial separation suggests electron transfer from the pyrene unit to the heptazine ring, accompanied by reverse hole transfer under excitation22. Thus, electron accumulation in the heptazine ring region may facilitate proton reduction and enhance the adsorption of metal cations in seawater. As displayed in Supplementary Table 7, the UPy2, U2Py2, and U3Py2 models showed larger oscillator strengths than the UCN model, which can be attributed to extended π-conjugation and D–A alignment. These features are expected to enlarge the transition dipole moment and contribute to stronger visible-light absorption, enhanced intramolecular fields, and more efficient charge separation, collectively leading to the observed improvement in PHE performance78.

Mechanism of PHE in seawater
To elucidate the origin of the high PHE performance of UPy2 in seawater, we examined its behavior in simulated seawater containing varying concentrations of NaCl and MgCl2 (Fig. 6a and Supplementary Fig. 58a, b). The volcano-shaped relationship between the hydrogen production rate and salt concentration indicates that the PHE performance was maximized at optimal NaCl and MgCl2 concentrations. Owing to their high concentration in natural seawater, Cl− ions can be oxidized to dissolved Cl2 and HClO, which are typically detected using their chromogenic reactions with KI5. However, no color change was observed upon the addition of KI to the post reaction mixture, which suggested the absence of these species, probably because of the suppressed electrostatic adsorption of Cl− on the UPy2 surface. Subsequently, Cl− was replaced with alternative anions. The comparable PHE rate obtained in a 5.1 wt% NaNO3 solution (which had a Na+ concentration equivalent to that of the 3.5 wt% NaCl solution) indicated the important role of Na+ in enhancing PHE (Supplementary Fig. 58c). Additionally, the PHE performance improved when DI water was spiked with metal cations at seawater-relevant concentrations (0.074 wt% KCl and 0.15 wt% CaCl2) (Supplementary Fig. 58d). This enhancement was ascribed to the coordination of these cations by the electron-deficient heptazine ring of UPy2, which promoted TEOA adsorption and accelerated hole consumption.

Given that cations tend to bind TEOA through ionic interactions with its –OH groups to form cation–TEOA complexes79, the adsorption behavior of these complexes on UCN and UPy2 was investigated using DFT calculations. The energies of Na+–TEOA (−1.24 eV) and Mg2+–TEOA (−2.27 eV) adsorption on UPy2 were substantially more negative than those observed for CN (−0.44 eV and −2.11 eV, respectively), indicating that the covalent linkage of Py2 to UCN enhanced the adsorption of both complexes (Fig. 6b, Supplementary Figs. 59–62, and Supplementary Data 8). This finding is consistent with an enhanced affinity of the heptazine units in UPy2 toward metal–triethanolamine complexes, which may be associated with increased electron density arising from intramolecular charge redistribution involving the pyrene moiety. The TD-DFT-based charge distribution analysis of Na+–TEOA and Mg2+–TEOA adsorbed on UPy2 indicated a tendency toward electron–hole separation, with electrons preferentially redistributed toward the heptazine ring under excitation (Fig. 6c, Supplementary Figs. 63 and 64, and Supplementary Data 9 and 10). This electron redistribution may enhance Na+–TEOA adsorption and promote charge separation. As a result, hole consumption by TEOA at both the Py2 and Na+–TEOA sites was facilitated, while proton reduction (and, hence, hydrogen generation) occurred at the UCN site. Collectively, these effects contributed to the high PHE performance of UPy2 in seawater. Because photogenerated holes are primarily localized on the pyrene core, the adsorption behavior of uncoordinated TEOA on Py2 and UPy2 was investigated. The adsorption energy of TEOA on UPy2 was slightly more negative than that of Py2 (Supplementary Figs. 65 and 66), suggesting that covalent linkage of Py2 to UCN enhanced hole accumulation at the pyrene core and facilitated TEOA adsorption. Moreover, TD-DFT-based charge distribution analysis of TEOA-adsorbed UPy2 showed a similar trend of excited-state charge redistribution, accompanied by an increase in local electron density around the heptazine ring (Supplementary Fig. 67 and Supplementary Data 11).

To further evaluate the TEOA adsorption capacity, we measured the zeta potentials of UCN and UPy2 in different solutions (DI water, DI–TEOA, and seawater–TEOA) at room temperature. UCN and UPy2 exhibited negative zeta potentials across all conditions (Supplementary Figs. 68 and 69). UPy2 showed a larger decrease in zeta potential (−9.5 mV) upon dispersion in DI–TEOA than UCN (−3.3 mV), thus featuring stronger TEOA adsorption despite having a two-fold lower specific surface area. When dispersed in seawater–TEOA, UPy2 exhibited a greater positive shift in zeta potential (+10.7 mV) than UCN (+5.5 mV), which confirmed the efficient ability of the former to adsorb metal cations from seawater. The enhanced TEOA adsorption was further supported by the results of total organic carbon (TOC) analysis (Supplementary Table 8), with the lower TOC content of UPy2 in seawater–TEOA indicating that the presence of salt ions enhanced TEOA adsorption80. Collectively, the theoretical and experimental results demonstrate that the covalent functionalization of CN with electron-donating pyrene units via π-bridges facilitates metal ion and TEOA adsorption, accelerates hole consumption, and enhances charge carrier separation in seawater.

The mechanism underlying the high PHE performance of UPy2 in seawater was further investigated by measuring its charge transfer and separation properties in different metal cation–containing solutions (NaCl, KCl, MgCl2, and CaCl2). Compared with that in DI water, UPy2 in metal cation–containing solutions exhibited a decreased PL intensity and shorter PL lifetimes (Fig. 6d, e and Supplementary Table 9), which indicated that metal cations facilitated the separation of photogenerated charge carriers. Additional PL measurements were conducted for UPy2 in DI water, seawater, and seawater containing TEOA. The PL intensity and lifetime decreased upon going from DI water to seawater, which was attributed to the adsorption of metal cations passivating radiative recombination centers on the UPy2 surface (Fig. 6f, g; Supplementary Table 10). The presence of TEOA in seawater further suppressed radiative recombination and enhanced charge separation in UPy2.

Finally, given the notably enhanced PHE performance of UPy2 in the MgCl2 solution, we examined the role of Mg2+ in the PHE process. The TEM imaging of UPy2 after PHE in seawater revealed the formation of ultrathin Mg(OH)2 nanosheets during the reaction (Supplementary Figs. 26 and 29). Although the Mg(OH)2 precipitate partially covered the PHE active sites of UPy2, the observed distribution of Pt nanoparticles on Mg(OH)2 suggests its electron-donating capability, as supported by the energy shift in the insitu Mg 1s spectrum after illumination (Supplementary Fig. 70). These findings indicate that Mg(OH)2 may also provide active sites for the PHE reaction. The role of Mg(OH)2 in charge transfer was examined using PL measurements under 365 nm excitation. Seawater-processed UPy2 exhibited the lowest PL intensity and fastest PL decay rate, which indicated that Mg(OH)2 precipitation promoted electron transfer and separation, thereby suppressing charge carrier recombination and reducing carrier lifetimes (Fig. 6h, i; Supplementary Table 11).
paper_content.methods:
Materials
Urea (CO(NH2)2, 99.5%), anhydrous ethanol (C2H6O, 99.8%), chloroplatinic acid hexahydrate (H2PtCl6·6H2O, Pt 37.5% min), sodium chloride (NaCl, 99.8%), magnesium chloride (MgCl2, 99%), potassium chloride (KCl, 99.99%), and calcium chloride anhydrous (CaCl2, 94%) were purchased from Shanghai Macklin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. 4,4′,4′′,4′′′-(Pyrene-1,3,6,8-tetrayl)tetrabenzaldehyde (Py1, 97%), 4′,4′′′,4′′′′′,4′′′′′′′-(Pyrene-1,3,6,8-tetrayl)tetrakis(([1,1′-biphenyl]-4-carbaldehyde)) (Py2, 98%), and 4,4′,4′′,4′′′-(Pyrene-1,3,6,8-tetrayltetrakis(ethyne-2,1-diyl))tetrabenzaldehyde (Py3, 95%) were obtained from Bide Pharmatech Co., Ltd. Acetic acid (C2H4O2, 99.8%), triethanolamine (C6H15NO3, 99%), and sodium nitrate (NaNO3, 99.0%) were purchased from Shanghai Aladdin Biochemical Technology Co., Ltd. All chemicals were used as received without further purification. Deionized (DI) water with a resistivity of 18.25 MΩ cm was used throughout the experiments.

Synthesis of ultrathin CN nanosheets (UCN)
CN was synthesized via thermal polymerization of urea. Typically, 30 g of urea powder was placed in a covered ceramic crucible (100 mL) and calcined in air at 823 K for 4 h with a ramping rate of 10 K min−1. The resulting yellow powder was collected as bulk CN. Ultrathin CN nanosheets (denoted as UCN) were then obtained by direct thermal oxidation etching of bulk CN (0.5 g) at 793 K for 6 h with a ramping rate of 10 K min−1. The final product was collected with an approximate yield of 20%.

Synthesis of UPy frameworks
UCN (0.1 g) was dispersed in 40 mL of anhydrous ethanol and ultrasonicated for 6 h. A solution of x mg Py2 in 10 mL of absolute ethanol was added dropwise to the suspension under stirring. Subsequently, 0.1 mL of acetic acid was added, and the resulting mixture was transferred to a thermostatic oil bath and refluxed at 353 K for 24 h under continuous stirring. After naturally cooling to room temperature, the product was centrifuged, washed with ethanol, and then freeze-dried for 48 h. The resulting samples were denoted as UPy2-x, where x indicates the mass of Py2. The UPy1-x and UPy3-x samples were synthesized following the same procedure as UPy2-x, using Py1 and Py3, respectively. For comparison, CPy2-3 was synthesized using the same method as UPy2-3, except that bulk CN was used instead of UCN. The UPy2-π-π composite, featuring interfacial π-π interaction, was synthesized by adding 5 mg of Py2 to the UCN suspension and stirring at room temperature for 24 h. The suspension was then centrifuged and freeze-dried for 48 h.

Characterization
XRD patterns were recorded using a Rigaku Ultima Ⅳ X-ray diffractometer using Cu Kα radiation (40 kV, 40 mA). FTIR spectra were acquired on a Vertex 70-Hyperion 3000 FTIR spectrometer using the KBr pellet technique. Solid-state 13C nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra were measured on a Bruker Ascend 600 MHz NMR instrument. Elemental analysis was performed using a Vario EL Cube elemental analyzer. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) images were obtained using a JEOL JSM-IT200A SEM and a Thermo Fisher Talos 200X G2 TEM (200 kV), respectively. Synchrotron-based X-ray spectroscopic measurements at the C and N K-edge were conducted at the Catalysis and Surface Science Endstation, beamline BL11U, at the National Synchrotron Radiation Laboratory, Hefei, China. Nitrogen adsorption-desorption isotherms were recorded using a Micromeritics ASAP 2460 3.01 instrument at 77 K, after degassing the samples at 393 K for 6 h. Specific surface area and pore volume were analyzed using the Brunauer-Emmett-Teller method. UV-vis diffuse reflectance spectra were recorded using a Techcomp UV-2600 spectrometer equipped with an integrating sphere. UPS spectra were acquired using a Thermo Fisher ESCALAB Xi+ spectrometer. Insitu XPS spectra were measured using a Thermo-VG Scientific ESCALAB 250 photoelectron spectrometer under λ≥400 nm light excitation. The C 1s signal at 284.80 eV was used as a reference for binding energy calibration. All XPS analyses were performed under high vacuum (P<10−9 mbar) with a pass energy of 100 eV for survey scans and 30 eV for high-resolution scans. TOC was measured by a Total Organic Carbon Analyzer (Shimadzu TOC-L). 10 mg of catalyst was dispersed into a 20 mL solution (DI water or seawater) containing 5 vol% TEOA by ultrasonication for 60 min. The resulting suspension was filtered by a 0.22 μm pore size membrane. 100 μL of filtrated solution was added to 30 mL DI water for TOC measurement. Photoluminescence (PL) emission quenching, PLQY, PL decay, and TD-PL spectra were collected using an Edinburgh FLS-1000 spectrofluorometer. The average lifetime (τavg), PLQY, and exciton binding energy (Eb) were calculated using the following Eqs. (1–3):

τavg = (A1τ1^2 + A2τ2^2) / (A1τ1 + A2τ2) (1)

PLQY = (RL / (ES - ER)) × 100% (2)

I(T) = I0 / (1 + k exp(-Eb / kBT)) (3)

where L is the emission spectrum of the sample; and ES and ER are the excitation light with and without the sample in the integrating sphere, respectively. I0 is the PL intensity at 0 K, kB is the Boltzmann constant. fs-TAS was conducted using a Helios pump-probe system (Ultrafast Systems LLC), coupled with a femtosecond laser system (Coherent). A 325 nm pump pulse (~0.1 μJ/pulse) was generated via a TOPAS-800-fs optical parametric amplifier, excited by a Ti:sapphire regenerative amplifier (Legend Elite-1K-HE, 800 nm, 35 fs, 7 mJ/pulse, 1 kHz) and seeded by a mode-locked Ti:sapphire laser system (Micra 5) and a Nd: YLF laser (Evolution 30). White-light continuum (WLC) probe pulses (350–650 nm) were generated by focusing 800 nm beams (400 nJ/pulse) onto a CaF2 plate. A reference beam was used to compensate for pulse-to-pulse WLC fluctuations. A motorized optical delay line controlled the pump-probe delay (0–8 ns). The instrument response function was determined to be 100 fs via cross-correlation. A mechanical chopper (500 Hz) modulated the pump pulses to acquire spectra alternately with and without excitation. For testing, 0.1 g L−1 samples were dispersed in ethylene glycol and loaded into quartz cuvettes with a 2 mm path length. SPV spectra were measured using a CEL-SPS1000 spectrometer. The BIEF magnitude was calculated using the Kanata model as follows (Eq. 4):

Fs = (ρ / εε0) * 2Vs (4)

where Fs denotes the magnitude of the BIEF, Vs stands for the surface potential, ρ stands for the surface charge density, ε is the low-frequency dielectric constant, and ε0 is the permittivity of free space. Because both ε and ε0 are constants, the magnitude of BIEF is governed by the values of ρ and Vs81. Electron spin resonance spectra of spin-trapped radicals (with 5,5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline n-oxide, DMPO, in methanol) were recorded using a Bruker EMX plus-6/1 spectrometer. KPFM was performed on a Bruker atomic force microscope equipped with a light irradiation system to assess surface morphology and potential. Zeta potentials of aqueous suspensions were measured via dynamic light scattering on a Malvern Zetasizer Nano ZS90.

Photocatalytic hydrogen evolution (PHE) test
PHE under negative pressure. PHE under negative pressure was conducted in a Pyrex reaction vessel maintained at 281 K, connected to a closed gas circulation system (Labsolar IIIAG, Beijing Perfectlight Technology Co., Ltd.; Supplementary Fig. 14). In a typical experiment, 10 mg of photocatalyst was dispersed in 100 mL of an aqueous solution containing 10 vol% triethanolamine (TEOA) as a hole scavenger. A 3 wt% Pt cocatalyst was deposited via insitu photo-deposition using H2PtCl6. A 300 W Xe lamp (Microsolar 300, Beijing Perfectlight Technology Co., Ltd.) equipped with a 400 nm cut-off filter was employed as the visible light source, with the irradiation intensity calibrated to ~100 mW cm−2. The amount of evolved H2 was quantified using a gas chromatograph (GC7900, TCD, Ar carrier gas). The H2 evolution curve under negative pressure is shown in Supplementary Fig. 15a.

PHE under ambient pressure. PHE under ambient pressure was carried out in a Pyrex vessel connected to a gas circulation system (Supplementary Fig. 18). The reaction temperature was maintained at 298 K using a cooling chiller. A 300 W Xe lamp with an AM 1.5G filter (Microsolar 300, Beijing Perfectlight Technology Co., Ltd.) served as the simulated solar light source, and the irradiation intensity was calibrated to ~100 mW cm−2. The corresponding simulated solar spectrum is provided in Supplementary Fig. 19. Gas samples (1 mL) were extracted hourly using a syringe and injected into the closed gas system for H2 quantification via gas chromatography (GC7900, TCD, Ar carrier). H2 evolution was measured under ambient pressure conditions to construct a calibration curve based on peak area, which was then used to determine H2 production during PHE measurements. The gas chromatography spectrum of H2, O2, and N2 is displayed in Supplementary Fig. 21. The H2 evolution curve under ambient pressure is shown in Supplementary Fig. 15b. Natural seawater was collected from the South China Sea (19°37.421′ N, 114°12.334′ E). The wavelength-dependent H2 evolution was investigated using a Microsolar 300 Xe lamp equipped with bandpass filters (λ=380, 420, 450, 475, and 500 nm). The light intensity was measured using a PL-MW2000 optical power meter and calculated by the five-point method. The distance between the probe and the xenon lamp was adjusted to match the distance between the Xe lamp and the liquid surface during the photocatalytic reaction (Supplementary Fig. 20)77. For AQE measurements, 20 mg of photocatalyst and a trace amount of H2PtCl6 were dispersed in 100 mL of DI water, 3.5 wt% NaCl solution, or natural seawater, each containing 5 vol% TEOA. The AQE was determined from a single experiment under steady-state conditions and calculated using the following Eq. (5); therefore, no statistical error analysis is provided.

AQE(%) = (2 × Number of H2 molecules) / (Number of incident photons) = (2 × RH2 × NA) / (S × P × t × λ / hc) × 100% (5)

RH2 represents the amount of produced H2 (μmol), NA is Avogadro’s constant, S denotes the illumination area, P and λ correspond to the intensity (W cm−2) and wavelength (nm) of the monochromatic light, respectively, t is the irradiation time (s), h is Planck’s constant, and c is the speed of light82.

PHE test in natural seawater under ambient pressure and natural sunlight was performed in a custom-built disk reactor made entirely of quartz with a top quartz window. The reactor had a diameter of 20 cm and a height of 10 cm. Approximately 40 mg of photocatalyst was dispersed in 200 mL of seawater containing 5 vol% TEOA and transferred into either the panel or disk reactor. On November 26, 2024, at 10:00 a.m., the solar irradiance was measured to be 95.5 mW cm−2. The evolved H2 gas was collected via the upward water displacement method (Supplementary Fig. 35).

Photoelectrochemical measurements. Photoelectrochemical measurements, including linear sweep voltammetry, transient photocurrent response, and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS), were performed using a CHI660C electrochemical workstation with a standard three-electrode configuration. A KCl-saturated Ag/AgCl electrode served as the reference electrode, and a platinum plate was used as the counter electrode. The working electrode was prepared as follows: 5 mg of the solid catalyst and 5 μL of 0.5% Nafion solution were ultrasonically dispersed in a mixture of 0.5 mL ethanol and 0.5 mL ultrapure water for 2 h. Subsequently, 5 μL of the resulting catalytic ink was drop-cast onto a L-type glassy carbon electrode and dried under an infrared lamp. A 0.5 M Na2SO4 aqueous solution (30 mL) was used as the electrolyte with the pH=6.8±0.2. Illumination (λ>400 nm) was provided by a 300 W Xe lamp (Microsolar 300, Beijing Perfectlight Technology Co., Ltd.). The transient photocurrent response was recorded under chopped light irradiation at 20-s intervals without applying an external bias. The linear sweep voltammograms curves were referred to the reversible hydrogen electrode (RHE): ERHE = EAg/AgCl + 0.197 + 0.0591·pH. EIS measurements were conducted in the dark over a frequency range of 0.1 to 105 Hz at the corresponding open-circuit potential. For EIS testing, the electrolyte consisted of a 1:1 mixture of 0.1 M K3Fe(CN)6 and K4Fe(CN)6 aqueous solution.

Theoretical calculations. The theoretical calculations were performed via the Gaussian 16 suite of programs. The geometric structures of the target molecules (CN, Py1, Py2, Py3, UPy1, UPy2, and UPy3) were optimized using the B3LYP-D3BJ functional with the 6-31G(d) basis set. Vibrational frequency calculations were performed at the same level of theory to confirm that all frequencies are real, thereby verifying that each structure corresponds to a local minimum on the potential energy surface. The molecular dipole moments were evaluated using the larger 6-311+G(d) basis set83. The Visual Molecular Dynamics program was used to plot the color-filled iso-surface graphs to visualize the molecular electrostatic potential. The HOMO and LUMO energy levels of CN and UPy models were calculated using DFT calculations with B3LYP functionals and a 6-31G (d, p) basis set. It should be noted that these DFT calculations are based on simplified molecular models and do not fully capture the structural complexity and dynamic catalytic environment of the actual materials. Therefore, the theoretical results are intended to provide qualitative insights into possible charge redistribution and electronic structure trends rather than a quantitative description under real catalytic conditions. Excited-state calculations were carried out using TD-DFT at the B3LYP/6-31G(d) level. Hole-electron analysis for the S1–S10 states was conducted using the Multiwfn program. The adsorption energy (ΔEads) was defined as the following Eq. (6):

ΔEads = Ead/sub − Ead − Esub (6)

where Ead/sub is the total energy of the optimized adsorbate/substrate system, Ead is the energy of the adsorbate in its isolated structure, and Esub corresponds to the energy of the clean substrate. A more negative Eads value generally indicates stronger adsorption.

The Gibbs free energy change (ΔG) was calculated according to Eq. (7):

ΔG = ΔE + ΔZPE − ΔTS (7)

where ΔG, ΔE, ΔZPE, and ΔTS represent the Gibbs free energy, the total energy change obtained from DFT calculations, the zero-point energy correction, and the entropic contributions (with T=298 K), respectively84. The change in Gibbs free energy of a molecule is calculated according to the following Eq. (8):

ΔG(ab) = ΔG(a) − ΔG(b) (8)

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this work, the authors report the synthesis of donor–π–acceptor (D–π–A) structured carbon nitride (UPy) frameworks by covalently linking ultrathin CN nanosheets to electron-donating pyrene units via various π-bridges. This design aims to achieve efficient photocatalytic seawater splitting under ambient pressure and natural sunlight. The study demonstrates that employing biphenyl moieties as π-bridges in D–π–A frameworks significantly reduce exciton binding energy and enhances electron delocalization and charge separation, thereby leading to an impressive hydrogen evolution rate of 134 mmol h⁻¹ g⁻¹. This result highlights the potential of the developed materials for practical solar-driven hydrogen production in natural seawater. Furthermore, the authors systematically investigate the influence of metal ions in seawater on the catalytic mechanism through a combination of control experiments, spectroscopic studies, and theoretical calculations. The work is representative and insightful in the field of photocatalytic water splitting. I recommend the publication of the manuscript in Nature Communications after minor revisions.
1. Electron delocalization is beneficial for the formation of the build-in electric field. Please quantify the intensity of the built-in electric field toward UCN and UPy frameworks in this work (Angewandte Chemie, e202507028; Applied Catalysis B: Environment and Energy 362, 124724).
2. In Figure S23, the UPy2 catalyst exhibits strong dependence on Pt loading, with optimal performance at 5 wt%. This is notably higher than the typical optimal loading (<3 wt%) for Pt in carbon nitride or other organic semiconductor-based photocatalytic systems. Why such a high Pt loading is effective here without causing performance degradation, the reasons should be specified.
3. To better understand the role of metal ions, it would be helpful to include additional DT-DFT charge distributions for Na⁺–TEOA and Mg²⁺–TEOA adsorbed on UPy2 (ACS Catalysis 14 (18), 13768-13780).
4. Hydrophilicity plays a crucial role in photocatalytic activity. The discussion should be provided, if possible, quantify the hydrophilicity differences between UCN and the UPy frameworks.
5. In Supplementary Figures 28 and 29, the authors confirm the formation of Mg(OH)₂ on UPy2 after PHE in seawater. Was Ca(OH)₂ also observed?
6. What are the PHE performances of the pure pyrene derivatives Py1–3 under ambient pressure in seawater? The data is needed for a better understanding.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this manuscript (#NCOMMS-25-66364-T), the authors synthesized a series of highly conjugated UPy frameworks through covalent incorporation of pyrene units and π-bridges into a carbon nitride backbone. Among these materials, UPy2 demonstrated the highest photocatalytic hydrogen evolution performance under ambient conditions, with rates of 82 mmol h-1 g-1 under simulated sunlight and 134 mmol h-1 g-1 under natural sunlight. Time-resolved photoluminescence (PL) and femtosecond transient absorption (fs-TA) spectroscopy revealed that UPy2—which features a biphenyl π-bridge—exhibits a significantly reduced exciton binding energy and promotes more efficient charge separation between the carbon nitride and pyrene units compared to both UCN and the other UPy frameworks. The study is interesting; however, the following critical concerns must be satisfactorily addressed before it can proceed to the next stage of evaluation.
1. The PL quantum yields (PLQYs) of all samples should be provided, as a low PLQY may lead to unreliable exciton binding energy (Eb) values derived from temperature-dependent photoluminescence measurements.
2. The analysis of the fs-TA kinetics for UCN (Fig. 5c) should be refitted, as the current fitting parameters provided in the figure fail to accurately reproduce the data due to the absence of a long-time constant (or offset). Without this component, a physically meaningful kinetic model cannot be properly established. Additionally, the kinetic scheme proposed for UCN in Fig. 5e is incorrect and requires revision.
3. The analysis of the fs-TA kinetics for UPy2 (Fig. 5d) also appears to lack a long-time constant (or offset), indicating that the current fitting parameters may be inadequate.
4. The pump energy density employed in the fs-TA kinetic measurements must be clearly specified, as PCN-based systems are known to exhibit strongly pump fluence-dependent kinetics (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 2019, 141, 11219). Given this dependence, the kinetic differences observed between UCN and UPy2 at high pump energy densities may not stem solely from structural differences. The authors should either conduct the fs-TA study under a relatively low pump energy density or provide pump-fluence-dependent kinetic data for both UCN and UPy2.
5. Although the authors employed FTIR, XPS, NMR, and NEXAFS to confirm the successful linkage of Py1, Py2, and Py3 to CN, additional Raman spectroscopy characterization would provide further supportive evidence.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Li and coworkers introduced pyrene (Py) structural units into carbon nitride (CN) via covalent linkage, achieving a maximum hydrogen production rate of 134 mmol h⁻¹ g⁻¹ in photocatalytic seawater splitting, which is an excellent result among g-C3N4-based photocatalysts. The author also discussed the promoting effects of metal ions in seawater on the catalytic process. These results are interesting. However, there are some main issues with the mechanism discussion in the manuscript that need to be addressed before I can recommend publication in Nature Communication.
1.The percentage content of the Py in UPy frameworks should be determined and stated. The naming (UPy-x) in the Synthesis Method section is related to the mass of Py, but no relevant discussion is found in the manuscript—maybe I am mistaken. In addition, the effect of different Py contents on the catalytic activity should be discussed.
2.The absorption edges of the UPy1-3 frameworks seem to exhibit a blue-shift compared with those of the single-component Py1-3. How to explain this? No significant emergence of new peaks or disappearance of old peaks is observed in the absorption spectra of UPy, which seems insufficient to support the donor-acceptor (D-A) charge transfer process claimed by the authors.
3.The hydrogen production activity of UPy is significantly higher than that of the single-component CN and Py. What is the significance of the covalent linkage between the two components in UPy for the enhanced activity? Would simply compositing Py and CN also lead to an improvement in catalytic activity?
4.For FIG. 5C and FIG. 5D, the corresponding R² values are not provided. From the graphs alone, the double-exponential fitting in FIG. 5C does not seem to be the most appropriate; a triple-exponential fitting might lead to other conclusions.
5.Could the transient absorption (TA) spectra of the three small molecules be provided?
6.The pump light wavelength for transient absorption spectroscopy is selected as 365 nm. Would the photophysical process under excitation at this wavelength differ from that under visible light excitation? Have experiments been conducted pumped by visible light?
7.DFT calculations provide the electron distribution of the excited states based on a model structure consisting of one heptazine ring segment and one Py molecule. The oscillator strength data of the corresponding excited states should be provided to understand the contribution of different excited states. In addition, have calculations been performed for the case where one Py molecule is linked to multiple CN segments?
8.Since the photogenerated holes are distributed on the pyrene core, shouldn't the adsorption of TEOA on pyrene be studied, rather than on the heptazine ring?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
This paper covalently linked ultrathin CN nanosheets to electron-donating pyrene units via different π-bridges. The optimal catalyst efficiently promoted photocatalytic seawater splitting under ambient pressure and natural sunlight, achieving a record hydrogen evolution rate of 134 mmol h−1 g−1. But, the core innovations of this paper raise several fundamental concerns. There is a suspicion that the narrative was constructed to fit the data rather than the other way around. Recommend rejection by considering the following issues:
1.A comparison between UCN (Fig. 2b) and UCN fragments (Fig. 2d) in SEM images should be conducted at the same magnification to more intuitively assess whether ultrasonication can effectively fragment the nanosheets. Otherwise, the core premise of this paper—which involves fragmenting CN and then linking the fragments with π-pyrene-π small molecules—would be invalidated.
2.​From a processing perspective, are the air-heating preparation method for CN and the oxygen etching method for UCN fundamentally different?​ If not, why is CN's preparation method simply called "air heating," while UCN's method is given a more academic-sounding name like "oxygen etching"? If they share the same essence, shouldn't urea air heating directly yield UCN? Did the authors artificially introduce catalyst preparation steps for the sake of narrative in the paper?
3.The BET data often exhibits significant variability—each measurement may yield different results, which does not necessarily imply structural differences between CN and UCN.
4.The video of Fig. 3g is quite interesting, but the observed bubbles could result from water vapor evaporation or air expansion due to light heating. A hydrogen test tube 'pop' experiment should be conducted to verify. If this system can indeed produce hydrogen at ambient pressure and under natural light, this work would be highly publishable in top-tier journals like Nature or Science.
5.UPy frameworks should also exhibit decent performance even without sacrificial agents and without expensive Pt loading, right?
6.How does the performance of CN or ucn composite with π-pyrene-π small molecules loading? Could it potentially match the excellence of UPy systems as reported in the literature?
7.The experimental data of XPS, BET, PL, FTIR, etc. data may inherently vary due to experimental conditions, and selective reporting risks overinterpretation. No comment.

Response #2: We sincerely thank the reviewer for pointing out the blue-shift of the
absorption edges in UPy1-3 relative to the single-component Py1-3. As displayed in
Fig. R2, comparison of the UV–vis DRS spectra of the π-pyrene-π molecules
(Supplementary Fig. 39) and the UPy frameworks (Fig. 4a) confirms that the UPy
materials exhibit slightly blue-shifted absorption edges relative to their molecular
counterparts. This behavior can be primarily attributed to the conformational restriction
and increased orbital localization induced by grafting the π-pyrene-π molecules onto
UCN. In their free molecular state, π-pyrene-π molecules possess considerable
conformational flexibility that allows partial π-electron delocalization, thereby
lowering the π→π* excitation energy. Covalent attachment of the π-pyrene-π molecules
to the UCN restricts their rotational and vibrational degrees of freedom, leading to
enhanced π-electron localization. This increased localization raises the π→π* excitation
energy, resulting in the observed blue-shift in the absorption edgesR18.
(right).
The absence of distinct new absorption bands or the disappearance of existing
bands in the UPy spectra does not contradict the presence of donor–acceptor (D–A)
charge transfer interactions. It is well-established that charge transfer states in D–A
systems often exhibit very small oscillator strengths and strongly overlap with local π–
π* transitions, so that no separate charge transfer absorption band can be resolved in
steady-state UV–vis spectra, particularly when the loading of π-pyrene-π molecules on
the UCN is relatively low (~2 wt%)R19. In the UPy frameworks, the red-shifted
absorption edges and modestly increased absorption intensities relative to UCN are
fully consistent with electronic coupling between the π-pyrene-π molecules and the
UCN framework. These observations support the presence of D–A charge transfer, even
though the spectral signatures are not strongly pronounced. This scenario closely
resembles low-loading acceptor systems, where clear charge transfer features emerge
only at higher loadings, while weak charge transfer character at low concentrations
manifests mainly as subtle spectral shifts and intensity changes rather than distinct new
bandsR20. Thus, despite the absence of a distinct charge transfer band, the observed
spectral shifts provide reliable evidence supporting D–A charge transfer interactions in
the UPy frameworks.

Response #3: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful question. The
markedly higher PHE activity of the UPy frameworks arises from the synergistic effects
enabled by covalent linkage between the π-pyrene-π units and the UCN framework.
These effects cannot be achieved by simply mixing the two components.
For single-component UCN, the low PHE performance mainly results from its
limited light-harvesting capability (<400 nm) and high charge recombination rate, as
demonstrated by the UV-vis DRS spectra (Fig. 4a) and PL spectra (Fig. 4g, h). Similarly,
the weak PHE performances of π-pyrene-π molecules are mainly attributed to their high
charge recombination, as demonstrated by the fs-TAS decay kinetics (Supplementary
Figs. 50, 51). In the UPy frameworks, Py units were uniformly covalently anchored to
the edges of UCN, which leads to several key improvements. First, the light absorption
capability of the UPy frameworks is enhanced due to the expansion of the π-conjugated
structure upon covalent incorporation of the π-pyrene-π molecules (Fig. 4a). Second,
the donor–π–acceptor architecture of the UPy frameworks enabled facile
intramolecular pyrene-to-CN electron transfer through an electron push-pull effect,
significantly lowering the exciton binding energy and promoting electron delocalization
and charge separation, supported by the DFT calculations (ESP distributions in Fig. 1d,
HOMO and LUMO distributions in Supplementary Figs. 2, 3), exciton dissociation (Fig.
4c-f), PL analysis (Fig. 4g, h), built-in internal electric field intensity (Fig. 4i), and
charge transfer kinetics (Fig. 5). Collectively, these results demonstrate that covalent
linkage is essential for activating and sustaining efficient intramolecular charge transfer
and separation, thereby accounting for the superior photocatalytic performance of the
UPy frameworks.
